builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: ProTok: Unified Protein Tokenization via Modular Multi-Codebook Quantization
summary: ProTok replaces separate per-modality protein tokenizers (independent sequence, structure, and function vocabularies) with a single modular multi-codebook product-quantized vocabulary that supports inference from any modality subset without retraining. Adoption costs the training of a new tokenizer and any downstream model over its tokens, plus integration of a non-standard vocabulary; reconstruction quality (0.939 lDDT) and multi-modal fusion add pipeline complexity relative to single-modality tokenizers. Failure modes include degraded performance on out-of-distribution proteins, dependence on the availability and quality of structural and functional annotations, and benchmark gains that may not transfer to a specific downstream design or retrieval workload.
rationale: The method targets protein sequence/structure/function modeling rather than LLM inference, training efficiency, or agent systems, so it falls outside the reader's production practice unless the team specifically builds protein design or retrieval pipelines, in which case its single-checkpoint, modality-flexible inference would merit small-scale testing.
technique: Unified multi-modal protein tokenization via product quantization

claims.statement: ProTok replaces separate per-modality protein tokenizers (independent sequence, structure, and function vocabularies) with a single modular multi-codebook product-quantized vocabulary that supports inference from any modality subset without retraining. Adoption costs the training of a new tokenizer and any downstream model over its tokens, plus integration of a non-standard vocabulary; reconstruction quality (0.939 lDDT) and multi-modal fusion add pipeline complexity relative to single-modality tokenizers. Failure modes include degraded performance on out-of-distribution proteins, dependence on the availability and quality of structural and functional annotations, and benchmark gains that may not transfer to a specific downstream design or retrieval workload.

A compact language model trained over ProTok tokens produces 52% designable sampled backbones versus 21% for a parameter-matched GeoBPE baseline; ProTok also ranks first on 21 of 28 StructTokenBench splits and reaches 0.939 lDDT reconstruction on CATH 4.2.
